# Module 14: Multidimensional Arrays And Stencil Computation

::: notes
This module uses a tested numerical refactoring to introduce ndarray. Keep the
mathematics simple and make the ownership of each view explicit.
:::

## Module Arc

- Establish a tested loop-based baseline
- Represent a field with `Array2`
- Select array regions with borrowed views
- Express a stencil with `Zip`
- Reuse storage with double buffering
- Verify that the refactoring preserves behavior

::: notes
The example belongs near the end of the course because it combines ownership,
methods, errors, testing, and numerical constraints.
:::

```text
source-code/heat-diffusion/

```

- Same CLI

## The Five-Point Stencil

```text
                 up
                  |
left ---- center ---- right
                  |
                down
```

```text
new = center + alpha * dt
      * (up + down + left + right - 4 * center)
```

::: notes
The outer grid points are fixed boundary conditions, so only the interior is
updated.
:::

## Stability Is An Application Constraint

```text
alpha * dt <= 0.25
```

- Unit grid spacing
- Explicit two-dimensional scheme
- Checked before the simulation starts

::: notes
Rust prevents invalid memory access here, but it cannot infer numerical
stability. This distinction matters in scientific software.
:::

## Owned 2D Storage

```rust
let grid = Array2::<f64>::zeros((grid_size, grid_size));
let (rows, cols) = grid.dim();

let center = grid[[rows / 2, cols / 2]];
```

- Shape belongs to the array
- Storage is rectangular
- Default layout is row-major

::: notes
Contrast this briefly with `Vec<Vec<f64>>`, where rows are separate allocations
and can have different lengths.
:::

## Baseline: Explicit Indices

```rust
for row in 1..rows - 1 {
    for col in 1..cols - 1 {
        new_grid[[row, col]] = self.grid[[row, col]]
            + self.alpha * dt
                * (self.grid[[row + 1, col]]
                    + self.grid[[row - 1, col]]
                    + self.grid[[row, col + 1]]
                    + self.grid[[row, col - 1]]
                    - 4.0 * self.grid[[row, col]]);
    }
}
```

`source-code/heat-diffusion/naive/src/heat_diffusion.rs`

::: notes
Open the real implementation in the editor. The loop is direct and
beginner-readable, which makes it a good reference implementation.
:::

## `s!` Describes A Region

```rust
let interior =
    grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1]);
```

```text
all rows:       ..
one row:        0
interior rows:  1..rows - 1
```

::: notes
The macro builds slice information; slice then creates a view that borrows the
array. No element data is copied.
:::

## Mutable Boundary Views

```rust
self.grid
    .slice_mut(s![0, ..])
    .fill(boundary_temperature);

self.grid
    .slice_mut(s![.., 0])
    .fill(boundary_temperature);
```

- Select one boundary
- Borrow it mutably
- Apply one operation to the region

::: notes
Show the corresponding loops in the naive version. The slice formulation
states which region may be mutated.
:::

## Circular Hot Spot

```rust
for ((row, col), temperature) in spot.indexed_iter_mut() {
    let dr = row.abs_diff(spot_radius);
    let dc = col.abs_diff(spot_radius);

    if dr.pow(2) + dc.pow(2) <= spot_radius.pow(2) {
        *temperature = spot_temperature;
    }
}
```

::: notes
The mutable view covers the smallest square containing the circle. Its indices
are local to that view, so the radius is also the local center coordinate.
:::

## Five Aligned Views

```rust
let center = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1]);
let up     = grid.slice(s![0..rows - 2, 1..cols - 1]);
let down   = grid.slice(s![2..rows,     1..cols - 1]);
let left   = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 0..cols - 2]);
let right  = grid.slice(s![1..rows - 1, 2..cols]);
```

::: notes
All five views have shape (rows - 2, cols - 2). At any shared view index, they
refer to one point and its four neighbors.
:::

## `Zip` Walks Them Together

```rust
Zip::from(self.next_grid.slice_mut(
        s![1..rows - 1, 1..cols - 1],
    ))
    .and(center)
    .and(up)
    .and(down)
    .and(left)
    .and(right)
    .for_each(|new, &c, &u, &d, &l, &r| {
        *new = c + factor * (u + d + l + r - 4.0 * c);
    });
```

::: notes
Use the real source for the complete closure. Zip handles aligned traversal;
the code still states the numerical formula explicitly.
:::

## Borrowing Shapes The Design

- Input views borrow `grid` immutably
- The output view borrows `next_grid` mutably
- Distinct fields can be borrowed at the same time
- An in-place stencil would change later inputs

::: notes
This is the ownership lesson. The algorithm naturally needs an old state and a
new state, and Rust makes those roles visible.
:::

## Double Buffering

```rust
pub struct System {
    grid: Array2<f64>,
    next_grid: Array2<f64>,
    alpha: f64,
}
```

```rust
std::mem::swap(&mut self.grid, &mut self.next_grid);
```

- Two allocations, reused for every step
- Current state and next state stay separate

::: notes
The fixed boundaries are initialized in both arrays. Only the interior is
overwritten during each step.
:::

## Fuse The Convergence Reduction

```rust
let new_value = c + factor * (u + d + l + r - 4.0 * c);
max_change = max_change.max((new_value - c).abs());
*new = new_value;
```

- Compute the update
- Measure its change
- Store it in one traversal

::: notes
This removes the extra pass that compared old and new grids. It is still
straightforward because max_change is a scalar local to the sequential Zip.
:::

## Return A Borrowed Array View

```rust
pub fn get_grid(&self) -> ArrayView2<'_, f64> {
    self.grid.view()
}
```

- Read-only access
- Shape and stride metadata
- Cannot outlive `self`
- No element copy

::: notes
Callers that only index or iterate barely change. The return type makes the
borrowed array interface explicit and does not transfer ownership.
:::

## Layout And Performance

- Row-major is the default for owned `Array2`
- Views may be strided and non-contiguous
- Syntax alone does not establish performance
- Benchmark representative release builds

::: notes
Do not claim that Zip is automatically faster. The refactor first improves the
array-level expression and removes repeated allocation; measurement remains
necessary.
:::

## Which Crate?

| Need | Starting point |
|---|---|
| NumPy-like arrays, slices, views | `ndarray` |
| Vectors, matrices, transformations | `nalgebra` |
| Dense linear algebra performance | `faer` |
| Existing native linear algebra stack | BLAS/LAPACK-backed crate |

::: notes
This is orientation, not an exhaustive ecosystem comparison. Dependency and
deployment constraints may decide the practical choice.
:::

2. Replace one loop with an array operation
3. Run that project's unit tests

5. Inspect any diff before continuing

::: notes
Make one conceptual change at a time. The second implementation can also serve
as the reference solution after participants attempt individual steps.
:::

## Module Takeaways

- Arrays own data; views borrow regions
- Mutable views make write regions explicit
- `Zip` aligns several same-shaped views
- Double buffering fits stencil semantics
- Tests protect both scientific properties and CLI behavior

::: notes
Close by connecting this example back to ownership: the borrowing rules are
not incidental here; they express the lifetime and mutation constraints of the
numerical algorithm.
:::
